{
    "id": "06-communication/audience-analysis",
    "title": "Audience Analysis",
    "category": "06-communication",
    "level": "basic",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Profile who will receive a message — their prior knowledge, stakes, and constraints — before deciding what to say and in what form to say it.",
    "body": "Audience Analysis Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most failed communication was written before anyone asked who would read it. This skill front-loads that question: name the audience precisely, establish what they already know and what is at stake for them, and let those facts decide depth, order, and channel. The profile constrains the wording, not the truth — it changes how something is said, never whether the substance gets stated. When to Use Use before sending anything consequential to a group you cannot see — documentation, announcements, incident notices, decision requests. Do not use the profile to stereotype individuals or to substitute imagined preferences for the purpose of the message; a profile guides wording, it does not license telling people only what they want to hear. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | What the audience should know or do afterward | | | | Yes | Roles, prior knowledge, stakes, and constraints of the readers | | | | No | Where the message will arrive, with format constraints | Procedure 1. Name the audience precisely: \"all users\" is not an audience, while \"first-time administrators configuring single sign-on\" is. 2. Establish the baseline: what the reader already knows, so the message starts where they are rather than where the author wishes they were. 3. Establish the stakes: what changes for the reader if they act, and what changes if they do not. 4. Decide depth per segment — background, working detail, or decision s ummary — because one message cannot be all three at once. 5. Choose the channel and format each segment actually reads, and record constraints such as length limits or review requirements. 6. Revisit the profile when feedback arrives, because audiences drift and a stale profile misroutes everything built on it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Segments with baseline knowledge, stakes, and constraints | | | | Per-segment decisions on depth, order, and channel | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed knowledge | Readers lack context the author took for granted | Start from the actual baseline of the audience | | Self-reference | Message organized around the author instead of the reader | Reorder sections around reader stakes | | Averaged audience | One compromise message serves no segment | Split by segment and depth | | Stale profiles | The audience changed since the last analysis | Revalidate against observed feedback | | Missing stakes | Readers cannot tell why it matters to them | State consequences for the reader early | Security and Authority Boundary Audience analysis is a distribution decision, and distribution is a boundary: the segments a message will reach must feed directly into what it may contain, and no segment broader than the intended trust level of the content may be added as a recipient. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of audience analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audience_analysis). 2. The PlainLanguage.gov guidelines on writing for the audience (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. When to Use Use whenever an incident is visible to anyone beyond the responders — customers, leadership, partner teams — and from the first acknowledgement, not from the moment of diagnosis.     "body": "Negotiation Category: Communication | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Negotiation is reaching agreement when parties' interests partly conflict. The reliable core is preparation: separating positions from interests, knowing your reservation value and best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA), and identifying differences that can be traded instead of split. This skill covers that preparation and the conduct of exchanges that produce precise, verifiable terms — without fabricating leverage or inventing concessions. When to Use Use when terms must be agreed with a party that has its own interests: scope and price discussions, vendor terms, resource allocation between teams. Do not use it to manipulate or deceive a counterpart; commitments made must be within your actual mandate. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Ranked underlying interests, not opening positions | | | | Yes | Hard limits: budget, deadline, authority scope | | | | No | Known interests and pressures of the other side | | | | No | What happens if no agreement is reached (BATNA) | Procedure 1. Convert each stated position into the interest behind it; list them in priority order. 2. Quantify the reservation value: the worst acceptable outcome, derived from constraints and BATNA, not from hope. 3. Inventory tradable differences: things cheap for you and valuable to them, and vice versa. 4. Propose packages across several issues rather than conceding issue by issue. 5. Test every emerging agreement against both sides' alternatives; an agreement worse than a party's BATNA will not hold. 6. Close with precise terms: who, what, when, and how verification happens. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Precise, verifiable commitments | | | | What was offered and traded, with rationale | | | | Whether the reservation value was breached | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Single-issue tunnel vision | Everything reduced to price or one headline term | Negotiate packages across multiple issues | | Fabricated leverage | Bluffs collapse and destroy trust when called | Represent only real alternatives and constraints | | Unverifiable agreement | Terms too vague to check delivery | Close with measurable terms and verification steps | | Ignored stakeholders | The counterparty's principal is not at the table | Confirm who can actually commit | | Sunk-cost drift | Conceding past the reservation value to save the deal | Recheck the reservation value before each concession | Security and Authority Boundary An agent negotiates only within an explicit mandate from its principal.     "description": "Rewrite technical statements so a busy reader needs no extra context — short sentences, concrete nouns, active verbs, and no jargon left undefined.",
    "body": "Plain Language Writing Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Plain language is not simplified thinking; it is text that survives first contact with a reader who has no reason to reread it. This skill works mostly by subtraction: state the point in one sentence, prefer words the reader already owns, split sentences that carry more than one idea, and cut hedges until a claim stands alone. Terms of art survive only when they are load-bearing, and then they are defined on first use. When to Use Use for mixed or non-specialist audiences — documentation, summaries, status updates, user-facing messages — wherever the reader cannot be assumed to share the vocabulary of the author. Do not strip precision that the audience needs; plain language is calibrated to its readers, and for a specialist audience the shared vocabulary is part of the clarity, not an obstacle to it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The passage to rewrite | | | | Yes | Who will read it and what they already know | | | | Yes | The single takeaway or action the reader should leave with | Procedure 1. Write the point in one sentence before touching the draft; if that sentence does not exist, the passage has no spine yet. 2. Replace each term of art with plain wording, or keep it and define it on first use when the term is load-bearing. 3. Split any sentence that carries more than one idea, and put the actor before the verb in each half. 4. Cut throat-clearing openings and stacked hedges; say the claim once and let it stand. 5. Pair every number with a reference point, because bare figures force the reader to supply the missing scale. 6. Reread as the target reader, and delete anything that survives only to comfort the author. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The plain-language version of the passage | | | | Kept terms of art, each with its plain definition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Simplified into vagueness | Plain wording dropped load-bearing precision | Keep the technical term and define it inline | | Audience mismatch | Text calibrated to the wrong prior knowledge | Fix the audience statement before rewriting | | Hedge fog | Qualifiers stacked until nothing is asserted | State the claim once, plainly | | Sentence sprawl | One sentence carrying three ideas | Split at idea boundaries | | Naked numbers | Figures with no comparison given | Attach a reference point to every number | Security and Authority Boundary Plain text travels: writing for a broad audience multiplies the chance a passage is quoted out of context, so a rewrite must not widen disclosure — anything sensitive stays in documents scoped to the audience that may see it, and the plain version inherits the classification of its source.
